Consciousness. This is the subjective, first-person experience of things—the felt quality of seeing red, tasting chocolate, or feeling pain. It is the hardest problem in philosophy: explaining how physical matter, specifically the brain, generates subjective experience, why it feels like something to have experiences, and how the immaterial mind relates to the material body. Philosophers distinguish phenomenal consciousness, which is what experiences are like, from access consciousness, which is having information available for reasoning and action. Though consciousness has been a perennial philosophical puzzle, it became acute in modern philosophy after Descartes made the thinking subject foundational and established what we now call the mind-body problem.

Phenomenal consciousness is the subjective quality of experience, often called qualia. The redness of red and the painfulness of pain are private, first-person, and difficult to convey to others or analyze objectively. David Chalmers formulated what is called the hard problem of consciousness. He asked why physical processes produce subjective experience at all. Why isn't the processing of visual stimuli purely unconscious, the way the filtering of unwanted noise is unconscious? This points to what philosophers call the explanatory gap—there seems to be a logical gap between objective, physical descriptions of the brain and subjective experience. Knowing all the neural correlates of pain doesn't seem to explain what pain feels like.

Physicalism, or materialism, holds that consciousness is ultimately physical, either identical to brain states or dependent on them. Yet how physics can generate the felt quality of experience remains obscure. Dualism, by contrast, proposes that consciousness is non-physical, a separate substance causally interacting with the body. This avoids the hard problem but raises what is called the interaction problem: how can a non-physical mind affect a physical body? Panpsychism offers another option: the view that consciousness, or proto-consciousness, is a fundamental feature of the physical world, present in all matter at some level. This avoids the hard problem but faces charges of implausibility and vagueness.

Functionalism defines mental states by their functional roles—their causes, effects, and relations to other mental states—rather than their intrinsic character. This fits consciousness into a physicalist framework but may ignore the qualitative, subjective dimension. It is important to distinguish the hard problem from what philosophers call the easy problems of consciousness—explaining behavioral and cognitive capacities like attention, memory, and discrimination. These are scientifically tractable; consciousness itself is not. Contemporary consciousness studies span philosophy, neuroscience, psychology, and artificial intelligence, but the core puzzle remains: how to bridge the gap between objective physical description and subjective experience.
